title: Crop planning: rotations and associations
summary: Master multi-year rotations and fast successions so you never exhaust the soil and can break disease cycles.

pages.title: Why alternate crops?
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pourquoi alterner les cultures ?

pages.title: Crop planning: how to alternate crops?
pages.text: This module gives you the keys to organize your crop rotations and successions in order to preserve soil fertility, limit diseases and secure your harvests.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Planification des cultures : comment alterner les cultures ?

pages.title: Understanding the concepts of crop rotation and crop succession
pages.text: Before planning your growing beds, let's clarify the difference between rotation over several seasons and succession over a short cycle.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Comprendre les notions de rotation et succession de cultures

pages.title: Rotation and succession: two complementary concepts
pages.text:
- **Rotation** (several seasons or years): this is the planned alternation of crops over several seasons or years, often to avoid soil exhaustion and to limit the diseases or pests specific to a plant family (e.g., tomato crop → carrot crop).
- **Succession** (one year or short cycle): this is the sequence of crops on the same space during one year or over short cycles (e.g., lettuce → radish → bush beans).
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Rotation et succession : deux notions complémentaires

pages.title: Why strict rotation is not essential in living soil
pages.text:
In our specific context of bio-intensive market gardening on living soil, **strict rotation** is not essential because:

- **The soil is continuously improved** (compost, permanent cover, organic inputs).
- **Weeds** (also called unwanted plants) are limited by rest periods and green manure crops.
- **Crop diversity** naturally reduces risks.

What matters most is a **well-thought-out succession** and a simple alternation between botanical families, root types and nutrient needs.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pourquoi la rotation stricte n’est pas indispensable en sol vivant

pages.title: Criteria for choosing crops
pages.text: Choosing a crop depends on the climate, market demand and the characteristics of the previous crop.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Critères pour choisir les cultures

pages.title: Taking the season and the market into account
pages.text:
Two first criteria guide your planning:

**The season**

Adapt the crop to the dominant climate of the season: cool season, hot season or rainy season (humidity-tolerant crops).

**The market and commercial strategy**

- Produce what sells well when demand is high.
- Diversify to spread risks.
- Alternate short-cycle crops (lettuce) and long-cycle crops (tomato).
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Tenir compte de la saison et du marché

pages.title: Choosing the next crop according to the previous crop
pages.text:
To choose the right crop to plant based on the previous crop, you need to know **three key criteria**:

1. **Botanical family**: you must change family.
2. **Root type**: you must alternate deep, shallow and taproot systems.
3. **Compost needs**: you must alternate heavy feeders and light feeders.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Choisir la culture suivante selon la culture précédente

pages.title: Why know botanical families and root types?
pages.text: Understanding these two agronomic characteristics helps protect your crops and make balanced use of the whole depth of the soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pourquoi connaître les familles botaniques et le type racinaire ?

pages.title: The value of botanical families and root systems
pages.text:
1. **Botanical families**: plants of the same family often share the same pests and diseases (e.g., late blight for Solanaceae) as well as the same nutrient needs.
2. **Root systems**: different root systems exploit different soil layers (surface or depth). Alternating shallow and deep roots helps balance the use of the soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour L’intérêt des familles botaniques et des systèmes racinaires

pages.title: Why know compost input needs?
pages.text: Not all crops take up the same amount of nutrients from the soil. Properly balancing the alternations avoids exhausting your growing beds.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Pourquoi connaître les besoins d’apports en compost ?

pages.title: Balancing compost needs
pages.text: Alternating **heavy-feeding crops** and **less demanding (light-feeding) crops** spreads the load on the soil and optimizes your compost inputs.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Équilibrer les besoins en compost

pages.title: Resources for planning alternations well
pages.text: To organize your beds without mistakes, you can rely on three practical reference tools.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Ressources pour bien planifier les alternances

pages.title: The three planning tools
pages.text:
To make your crop choices easier and avoid risky successions, rely on three main tools:

1. **Crop combination tables**: indicate recommended and discouraged successions. They allow you to plan quickly starting from the crop currently in place.
2. **Plant technical sheets**: give compost needs, cycle length and disease susceptibility. They help you decide which crop can follow depending on the season, the soil and the market.
3. **Plant classification table**: classifies crops by botanical family and root type. It is used to avoid planting crops that are too closely related or with root systems that draw on the same soil layers.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les trois outils de planification

pages.title: Examples of successions: alternations to avoid
pages.text: Let's now look at the most common mistakes in crop sequencing and why they weaken your beds.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Exemples de successions : alternances à éviter

pages.title: The risks of a poor succession
pages.text:
Some crop successions **deplete the soil** or promote the appearance of **diseases** (fungi, bacteria, viruses) and **pests**.

⚠️ **Warning**: here are the four main mistakes to avoid in order to preserve the health of your growing beds.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les risques d’une mauvaise succession

pages.title: Alternations to avoid: monoculture and same family
pages.text:
1. **Monoculture**: growing the same plant several times in a row on the same space. This depletes the soil in a targeted way and favors diseases and pests specific to the crop (e.g., clubroot of cabbage, onion fly).
2. **Alternating between plants of the same botanical family**: even if the plants are different, they often share the same pests and diseases (e.g., two Solanaceae or two Cucurbitaceae in a row).
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Alternances à éviter : monoculture et même famille

pages.title: Alternations to avoid: same roots and overly demanding crops
pages.text:
3. **Alternating between plants with the same root type**: the same root type (spreading roots, fine shallow roots, etc.) draws on the same soil depth and often shows the same weaknesses to pests.
4. **Alternating between two very demanding crops**: following one nutrient-hungry crop with another, without rest or green manure, severely exhausts the soil. Both require a lot of compost, water and care.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Alternances à éviter : mêmes racines et cultures trop exigeantes

pages.title: Examples of successions: recommended alternations
pages.text: Conversely, some simple combinations durably strengthen the fertility of your beds and limit disease pressure.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Exemples de successions : alternances recommandées

pages.title: The benefits of a good succession
pages.text:
A good succession promotes **soil health**, limits **diseases** and optimizes the use of resources (water, compost, labor).

Here are the five principles to follow, with concrete examples.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Les bénéfices d’une bonne succession

pages.title: Recommended alternations: botanical family and root type
pages.text:
1. **Change botanical family**: alternating families (e.g., Solanaceae → Fabaceae; Solanaceae → Asteraceae; Liliaceae → Apiaceae) helps break specific disease and pest cycles.
2. **Change root type**: alternating fine shallow roots, taproots and tubers draws on different soil depths and improves soil structure.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Alternances recommandées : famille botanique et type de racine

pages.title: Recommended alternations: needs, duration and legumes
pages.text:
3. **Alternate heavy-feeding and light-feeding crops**: this avoids exhausting the soil and spreads compost and water needs (e.g., heavy feeder → moderate feeder → light feeder or nitrogen fixer).
4. **Insert a fast crop between two long ones**: this optimizes time and space while giving the soil a "relative rest" (e.g., long → short → long).
5. **Introduce a nitrogen-fixing legume**: Fabaceae (as green manure or harvested) enrich the soil with nitrogen, which benefits the following crops.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Alternances recommandées : besoins, durée et légumineuses

pages.title: Special cases and useful exceptions
pages.text: In practice, not all crops have the same constraints. Some offer more flexibility in your calendar.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Cas particuliers et exceptions utiles

pages.title: Low-impact crops and buffer crops
pages.text:
Some crops partly escape the general rules of alternation. Here are two types of cases to know:

1. **Low-impact crops (tolerant of repetition)**: some very short-cycle plants that are undemanding and not very susceptible to diseases can be grown twice in a row without great risk, if the soil remains fertile and healthy (especially by adding compost or a short rest in between).
2. **Buffer or transition crops**: some plants are considered neutral because they have few requirements, provide good soil cover, are not very susceptible to diseases and do not belong to problematic families. They can be used as a transition crop between two more demanding or risky crops.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Cultures à faible impact et cultures tampon

pages.title: Another approach: the simple seasonal strategy
pages.text: Discover a pragmatic method that is particularly well suited to local climate variations.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Autre approche : la stratégie saisonnière simple

pages.title: Planning with a simple seasonal strategy
pages.text:
Another planning strategy consists of planting **one main crop per season**. You choose a crop suited to the climate, then change in the following season.

The main advantages are:

- **Suited to local climatic conditions**.
- **Fewer diseases** thanks to the alternation of seasons.
- **Simplified planning**.

Even if some successions do not follow the classic rules of alternation, the change of season is often enough to break disease cycles. Remember to include a **green manure** or a **mulched rest** every 2 to 3 cycles.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Planifier avec une stratégie saisonnière simple

pages.title: Green manures and soil rest: useful breaks
pages.text: To keep a soil alive and productive over the long term, it is essential to include regeneration phases between your crops.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Engrais verts et repos du sol : des pauses utiles

pages.title: The role of green manures
pages.text:
**Green manures** are crops sown specifically to cover, structure and enrich the soil (legumes, millet, sorghum, etc.), then cut and left in place or used as mulch.

Together with rest periods, they are essential for keeping the soil alive and fertile:

- **Protect against erosion**, structure the soil and provide organic matter.
- **Break disease cycles**.
- **Smother unwanted plants** and slow the germination of weed seeds, especially when the compost applied is not fully mature.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Le rôle des engrais verts

pages.title: The active rest period
pages.text:
The **active rest period** consists of letting the growing bed regenerate without production:

- **Mulching without a crop** for **1 to 2 months**.
- **Soil regeneration**: breaks disease cycles and provides organic matter through the mulch.
- **Plastic mulching (optional)**: using a tarp speeds up the composting of the mulch, keeps moisture in the soil and prevents unwanted plants. A **black tarp** warms the soil, whereas a **white tarp** limits warming and keeps the temperature cooler.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour La période de repos actif

pages.title: When to include a green manure or a rest period?
pages.text:
Include a **green manure** or a **rest period** at the most favorable times:

- **Between two demanding crops**.
- **In a difficult season** (heavy rains or intense heat).
- **After 2 or 3 crop successions**.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Quand intégrer un engrais vert ou une période de repos ?

pages.title: Key takeaways: the three principles of good alternation
pages.text:
Good alternation rests on **three simple principles**:

1. **Change botanical family**.
2. **Vary the root type**.
3. **Balance the soil's needs**.

Adapt your strategy to the season, the duration of the crops and the condition of the soil. Remember to include, whenever possible, breaks with **green manures** or **mulched rest** to naturally regenerate the soil.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour À retenir : les trois principes d’une bonne alternance
